extracted.intended_audience: high-school English/art teachers and creative-writing educators
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, classroom-level guidance (embedded in fiction) for running combined poetry-reading-and-painting sessions with underprivileged high-school students—selection of poems, classroom tone, feedback practice, and follow-up with individual students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select accessible poems that appeal to students
rubrics_metrics.description: “He tried to select poetry from the high school reader that would appeal to them. This afternoon he was going to read some Robert Frost. He felt it would make sense to them, offer them images they could instinctively grasp.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose poems with concrete images and cultural resonance for the students so they can readily visualize and respond; prefer material from readers or poets likely to connect with their experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use painting as a means for students to express responses to poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “This afternoon he was going to read some Robert Frost... This would serve several functions: they will hear some poetry, they will express themselves in the paintings and, maybe... I can get through to them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair reading with an art activity so students can externalize interpretation nonverbally; the dual activity aims to increase exposure to poetry and provide a channel for personal expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hovering while students create to prevent inhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was Mr. Shapiro’s practice not to bother the students while they were painting, he felt his looking over their shoulders might inhibit or intimidate them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give students privacy and autonomy during creative work; step back to reduce performance anxiety and allow authentic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small tangible rewards thoughtfully to encourage
rubrics_metrics.description: “In September he had found a box of gold stars... Each week he pasted a star on a painting, trying to give the star where he felt it would do the most good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, visible tokens of recognition to motivate and validate students, placing praise where it will boost confidence rather than merely reward technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit and explain exemplary student work (usual practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The usual practice was to exhibit the best painting at the front of the room, and explain why it was the best.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly showcasing a student’s work and articulating reasons models criteria for quality and gives positive reinforcement; be mindful when deviating from this routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read poetry slowly and with emotion to engage students
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mr. Shapiro read the whole poem, slowly and with emotion. Now that the poem was fresh in his mind he recited most of it from memory.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver poems at an unhurried pace with expressive emphasis; repetition and familiarity (reciting from memory) can deepen impact and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep explanatory context brief to maintain attention
rubrics_metrics.description: “He started to explain further the irony... and felt he was losing the class again, so he cut it short.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When students’ attention flags, favor concise contextual remarks over extended lectures; prioritize engagement over exhaustive analysis in mixed-ability settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt approachable classroom manner to reduce resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: “He had read somewhere that a teacher in shirtsleeves provokes less resistance in these students.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small choices in dress and demeanor can lower barriers between teacher and students; be intentionally approachable to create a safer atmosphere for participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to leave students briefly unattended when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was not the standard procedure, leaving a class alone,... but he had done it before on Fridays and there were never any complaints.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For low-risk activities, periodic brief absence can foster student responsibility and trust—use discretion and know school rules/risks before leaving a classroom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider students’ home circumstances when assigning/display tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Jaime: “We live in a room with four other families... I want to hang my painting but I have no wall.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and accommodate material or spatial constraints in students’ lives; recognize that some creative outputs may have limited practical value to them and adapt expectations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up privately and compassionately with students in distress
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Shapiro walks Jaime home, buys him a hot chocolate, listens as Jaime explains why he cried about having no wall to hang his painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a student shows emotional distress, make time for private, empathetic follow-up—offer listening, small comforts, and a chance to explain rather than public interrogation.
